claims.text: The system consists of sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
Carbothermal-shock synthesis can produce nanoscale multielement particles with initially uniform elemental distributions and diameters as small as 3 nm.
The initial Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt particles are a homogeneous solid solution or a kinetically trapped mixed state.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down below a critical particle diameter of approximately 5 nm.
Below the critical size, surface-to-volume effects drive rapid segregation and Ostwald ripening rather than retention of an entropy-stabilized solid solution.
The proposed thermal treatment is a vacuum ramp from 300 K to 1000 K at approximately 10 K/min.
The surface diffusion coefficient and surface-energy anisotropy scale inversely with particle radius.
At sub-10 nm sizes, high curvature and large surface-to-volume ratio lower the activation energy for surface diffusion.
Enhanced surface diffusion enables rapid atomic migration during heating.
Au and Pt have sufficiently low surface energies to segregate to particle surfaces or migrate to larger particles.
Co and Cu tend to segregate toward particle cores or form distinct phases.
Structural evolution is driven primarily by minimization of total surface free energy rather than maximization of configurational entropy.
Heating will produce a bimodal size distribution, disappearance of particles smaller than 5 nm, and growth of larger particles.
Heating will produce core-shell or multiphase particles with Au/Pt-enriched surfaces and Co/Cu/Ni-enriched cores.
The heated particles will not retain the single-phase structure associated with a sluggish-diffusion signature.
An ideal equiatomic five-component alloy has a configurational mixing entropy of approximately 1.61 R.
High configurational entropy and sluggish bulk diffusion are expected under conventional HEA theory to suppress phase separation and growth up to 1000 K.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk diffusion should dominate and preserve a single-phase structure through sluggish-diffusion stabilization.
Residual carbon from synthesis could alter surface-diffusion kinetics.
Retention of a homogeneous single phase with no significant size redistribution or elemental segregation at 1000 K would falsify the proposed surface-driven mechanism.
